title: Public Value at Risk: How Quantum Power Becomes Systemic Risk in Global Finance
content: The capacity to break today’s public-key cryptography is concentrating in a few states and firms, while the financial systems that depend on it are interdependent. Because encrypted data can be HNDL once a cryptographically relevant quantum computer exists, part of the risk is already embedded in payments, credit records and public-finance records. This article examines how shifts in technological power become systemic financial risk. It develops three stylized models (harvest-now, decrypt-later exposure; myopic investment; weakest-link migration in a core-periphery network in which fragmentation costs fall with institutional quality, calibrates them illustratively and solves the network game numerically. Under a 5–15-year arrival window, records requiring confidentiality for ten years or more face exposure probabilities of 0.70 to 1.00. Accountability horizons shorter than the earliest plausible arrival remove the private incentive to invest. In the simulated network, support targeted at low-quality jurisdictions restores most protection when budgets are small and fragmentation is moderate. At high fragmentation, the margin shifts to core banks, and uniform or core-first allocations can perform as well or better. The article proposes a Post-Quantum Public Value Scorecard for supervisors, banks and treasuries, applies it to Portugal and treats quantum readiness as a supervisable dimension of systemic resilience.
